newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. gives Indian broadcast bill mixed grades.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gives Indian broadcast bill mixed grades.

text.p: The top U.S. communications regulator praised India's broadcasting bill for proposing to open up the airwaves but said a provision requiring all television firms to transmit from India was troublesome.
Federal Communications Commission chairman Reed Hundt said he was heartened by a clause in the draft legislation that would create many more television licences.
"The multiplying of broadcast outlets is good for consumers and good for democracy," Hundt told a group of reporters during an official visit to the Indian capital.

The U.S. regulator, who met senior Indian officials including Finance Minister P. Chidambaram this week, said television was crucial to advertising, which in turn helps spur consumer demand and economic growth.
"There is substantial unmet consumer demand in India. Broadcasting is crucial to tapping that demand," he said.
Hundt said the broadcast bill, which has been referred to a parliamentary committee and is expected to come to a vote by year's end, could create hundreds of new television licences.
India's private broadcasters currently have to rent time slots on state television or beam through satellites from abroad. They cannot own broadcast stations.

The bill would permit the auctioning of licences, which Hundt said could bring a large amount of money into the Indian government's coffers. He said the FCC had collected $11.7 billion through licence auctions.
"With 950 million people, even with very low prices per person, India could raise an awful lot of money," Hundt said.
The regulator said a clause limiting foreign equity stakes in broadcasters to 49 percent was not worrisome.

Indian Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy said on Thursday that a foreign stakeholder could effectively control a company even with 49 percent stake if the Indian shareholders were disparate.
But Hundt criticised a provision that would require all broadcasters to uplink, or transmit, from Indian soil.
"One provision is very troublesome -- the requirement that uplinking facilities be in this country," he said.
The U.S. regulator said that if every nation had that requirement, international broadcasters would have to have hundreds of uplinking facilities around the globe when only a handful were needed.
Hundt cited a U.S. agreement with Mexico that allows U.S. satellites to beam images into Mexico and vice versa.
"We don't care where the uplinking facility is," he said. "The purpose is to maximise the video market."
The current Indian bill would bar foreign investors from terrestrial, or local, broadcast companies.
Hundt said he anticipated modifications in the bill. "This is the early going and changes are in store," he said.
